the SIR methods are capable of improving the image quality of the FBP reconstructions for low-dose clinical CT scans, but the improvement is task-specific and depends on the choice of the statistical models and regularization strategies used in the objective function of SIR.
the statistical model of projection measurements and regularization strategy are both important for the success of SIR methods for CT.

there is not a single best statistical model or regularization strategy for low-dose SIR, but rather the choice of statistical model or regularization term should be based on the characteristics of projection data, the expected properties of images to be reconstructed, and the specific task of image reconstruction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the SIR methods have the potential to improve the image quality and clinical performance of low-dose CT as compared to the FBP method for a variety of clinical tasks.
the pML-based methods are more suitable for low-dose transmission X-ray CT, while the PWLS-based methods are more appropriate for low-dose cone-beam CT.
the pML and PWLS methods can be considered to be the most accurate statistical model-based SIR methods for the reconstruction of low-dosage CT images.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the SIR methods have great potential to improve image quality for low-dose and/or limited-view X-ray CT, but the success of the SIR depends on the accuracy of the statistical model and the choice of the regularization term.

the statistical model on the projection measurements and the regularization strategy are complementary and should be carefully designed for successful image reconstruction in a specific clinical task.
the statistical models on CT projections and the regularization strategies are highly correlated.
